pr_title: repart: Add support for formatting verity partitions
pr_body:
This commit adds a new Verity= setting to repart definition files
with two possible values: "data" and "hash".

If Verity= is set to "data", repart works as before, and populates
the partition with the content from CopyBlocks= or CopyFiles=.

If Verity= is set to "hash", repart will try to find a matching
data partition with Verity=data and equal values for CopyBlocks=
or CopyFiles=, Format= and MakeDirectories=. If a matching data
partition is found, repart will generate verity hashes for that
data partition in the verity partition. The UUID of the data
partition is set to the first 128 bits of the verity root hash. The
UUID of the hashes partition is set to the final 128 bits of the
verity root hash.

Fixes https://github.com/systemd/systemd/issues/24559
pr_comments:
cc @poettering 

This "assigns" data partitions to a verity partition so that a data partition can only be assigned to a single verity partition. I did this because if you have two identical root partitions and two identical verity partitions, the two verity partitions will both match the first root partition and so there won't be any verity partition for the data in the second root partition (which won't have the same root hash as the first root partition due to mkfs magic).

What we could also do is ensure that those two root partitions have the same root hash by checking if there's an identical partition when populating partitions and copying from that partition if one is found instead of running mkfs again. As of now this PR skips running mkfs again when generating the verity partitions, but maybe we should do it for identical regular partitions as well. That would remove the need for matching verity partitions to unique data partitions since identical data partitions will have the same root hash.

Let me know which you prefer.

Please also see the late suggestions:
https://github.com/systemd/systemd/issues/24559#issuecomment-1237804045
https://github.com/systemd/systemd/issues/24559#issuecomment-1237806934

issue_context.title: repart: Add support for formatting verity partitions
issue_context.body:
### Component

systemd-repart

### Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe

Currently, users are required to manually run `veritysetup format` after running repart to format any verity partitions. Ideall,y repart should be able to do this for the user.

### Describe the solution you'd like

Add support for a new `Verity` section to repart definitions files, providing a way to configure and format a verity partition for the given partition. If the `Verity` section is provided, repart will generate a verity partition for the current partition. The settings in the `Verity` section can be used to configure the generated Verity partition. 

### Describe alternatives you've considered

_No response_

### The systemd version you checked that didn't have the feature you are asking for

main
comments: So originally my focus for repart was to run at boot, and readjust partitions on the deployment machine. There it doesn't make too much sense to generate verity, since that's a job for an OS builder, not something you'd run on the deployment machine. But of course, the focus shifted a bit: repart is useful for building images too, on the OS builder's machine. So I guess adding this functionality would make sense, and I guess wouldn't even be that much code.

I'm a little unsure about the implementation. First, I was thinking along the lines of an optional `Verity` section that defines a verity partition for the regular partition defined in the same definition file. But then you'd have to duplicate many settings of the `Partition` section in the `Verity` section as well.

Then I figured we can add the `Verity` section to configure additional verity settings for a definition file defining a verity partition. But what I'm not sure about is how to specify the data partition for the verity partition in that case, the UUID is the closest to an identifier but when we're doing verity the UUID comes from the root hash so it's not defined yet for the data partition. The type can be ambiguous so I'm not sure that would be great either. We could do ordering based and use the previous partition as the data partition but that doesn't seem amazing either.

We could also use the definition file name as a match I guess (similar to unit file names which are also used as matches), but that would prevent us from making a verity partition of any partition that can't be matched against a definition file.

Any other ideas on how to specify the data partition for the verity partition? Or should we define data and corresponding verity partitions in the same definition file after all?

So what do you intend to use as source here for the whole op? i.e. have a ready made fs image that you want to generate a disk image from and then also add a verity partition for? i.e. CopyBlocks= in one partition? In that scheme things would be easy, you could just add VerityBlocks= or so and then have a pair of partitions: one with CopyBlocks= (for the payload) and one with VerityBlocks= (for the verity hashes). And then the UUID= setting would also learn two new magic values "verity-hi" and "verity-lo" or so, for the high/lo bits of the verity root hash of the CopyBlocks=/VerityBlocks= stuff. (of course, this means some caching would be needed to ensure we don't run the verity stuff twice, but just once).

i.e.:

50-root.conf:
```
[Partition]
Type=root
UUID=verity-lo
CopyBlocks=rootfs.data
```

60-root-verityconf:
```
[Partition]
Type=root-verity
UUID=verity-hi
VerityBlocks=rootfs.data
```
(and if there are other tweaks to verity people really want to make then add further VerityXYZ= fields to [Partition])

The issue is that I don't have a ready made image, I have a directory tree that I'll copy into partitions using CopyFiles. But verity works on blocks, so I'd like to use the repart generated data partition as the data device for the verity partition, but to do that I need a way to specify that generated data partition by repart in the definition file for the verity partition. I'm just not sure what the best way is to specify that.

repart would then generate all the partitions, copy the files in there if CopyFiles is specified, and as the final step, format the verity partition based on the data partition and somehow communicate the resulting roothash to the user. Probably by just writing to a file in the directory that repart is running from or so.

Hmm, I guess we could do it the same way for CopyFiles=. I mean, we try very hard to generate file systems reproducibly already, i.e. derive uuid/label in a stable way. We can build on that, and simply say that as long as you specify the same data for the fs we generate we'll cache the resulting fs binary data stuff for you, so that we can reuse it for the verity generation

i.e. let's say you have:

50-root.conf:

```
[Partition]
Type=root
UUID=verity-lo
CopyFiles=/my/source/tree
```

60-root-verityconf:

```
[Partition]
Type=root-verity
UUID=verity-hi
VerityFiles=/my/source/tree
```

i.e. if we you run stuff like this, then once we come to generate the data for the first of the two partitions we'll notice we haven't generated that so far, so we generate the fs for it. if the first partition was the non-verity one, we just copy that into the partition, but we also maintain a cache that uses the copy source path (and some of the relevant other settings, i.e. fstype and so on) as key. And then, when we come to the second partition, we look into that cache. And then instead of generating the fs new, we just use that again.

i.e. cache key would by copy source path + fstype + … and the cache value would be triplet of fd + offset + size, pointing to where the prepared data can be read from. We'd keep the cache open for the whole operation and close it only when done. Thus, as long as you use the exact same source path and parameters we'll always only run mkfs/copy once.

I think this would be really nice and simple. I mean, the mkfs/copy stuff isn't *truly* reproducible (because we are using kernel fs drivers here), but superficially they'll look the same, because same contents and same metadata. And by employing the cache we can both optimize generation (because we don't have to genreate the fs twice) but also get bitwise identical copies even though running mkfs/copy twice wouldn't actually give us that.

This would ensure things remain nicely independent conceptually (since the .conf files on paper are still entirely indepndent of each other) but things would be fast and systematic.

Does that make sense?
(I guess the next step would then to teach repart to generate squashfs too)

How would we derive the cache key from the verity partition config? Would we just have to duplicate the relevant settings from the data partition (Format=, Encrypt=, MakeDirectories=)?

But then that configuration wouldn't actually be configuration for the partition, but it'd just be there to make sure we can find the correct cache entry, so we'd have to add checks everywhere to not actually apply any of those settings if `VerityFiles` is also specified. That seems somewhat ugly to me.

I guess we could add `VerityFormat=`, `VerityEncrypt=` and `VerityMakeDirectories=` to indicate that those are only to match in the filesystem cache and don't actually apply to the partition.

I'm still not sure if I like having to duplicate all the configuration between the two but that's the price of keeping the definition files independent from each other I guess.

> I guess we could add `VerityFormat=`, `VerityEncrypt=` and `VerityMakeDirectories=` to indicate that those are only to match in the filesystem cache and don't actually apply to the partition.

Well, VerityEncrypt= doesn#t really make sense conceptually... Encryption *and* verity sounds a bogus concept to me. I'd refuse that.

But maybe you have a point. Instead of Adding VerityFiles= we maybe should instead just make it a new setting Verity=yes|no (with "no" — which should be the default — you get the behaviour as now. But if yes, then we'll simply store the the verity hashes of what is defined here, and then doing the caching as suggested.

Implementation-wise we should probably add another phase to the whole thing, so that we have one phase where we mkfs/copy all data, and then a second phase where we then generate the hash data from it.

> I'm still not sure if I like having to duplicate all the configuration between the two but that's the price of keeping the definition files independent from each other I guess.

It's not thaaaat much. But I guess it means we should normalize things to minimize risk of fucking this up. i.e. sort MakeDirectories= arguments and so on while parsing.

So to summarize, maybe this:

50-root.conf:
```
[Partition]
Type=root
UUID=verity-lo
CopyFiles=/my/source/tree
MakeDirectories=a b c
Format=xfs
```

60-root-verity.conf:

```
[Partition]
Type=root-verity
UUID=verity-hi
Verity=yes
CopyFiles=/my/source/tree
MakeDirectories=a b c
Format=xfs
```

And then in one of the two phases we process 50-root.conf and generate the fs for the root. And then in the second phase we process 60-root-verity.conf and see the Verity=yes setting, and then look up in our cache if we already built an fs with this data, and use it then, and simply generate the verity data for it.

Hmm, thinking one step further: we support embedded PCKS#7 sigs for verity root hases in another partition these days, so maybe instead of Verity=yes|no we should make it an enum instead, so that you can pick

```
Verity=data
Verity=hash
Verity=signature
```

And the default woud be `Verity=data`, i.e. we actually format/copy files. But Verity=hash is set we'd generate the hash blob and write that instead, based on the cached fs image. And if Verity=signature we'd generate the PKCS7 signature and write that. The cache would thus no only carry info about generated file systems, but also about the root hash. And we'd have a three-phase process: first, iterate through all partitions to generate any filesystems/populate them. And then, iterate through all partitions again, generating verity data. And then iterate a third time, generating signatures.

And I'd probably make things simply fail if people use Verity=hash but never used Verity=data with the same parameters on some other partition. And similar, if people use Verity=signature but have no Verity=data partition elsewhere.

(I mean, I am not suggested you implement the pkcs#7 right-away – of course you#d be more than welcome –, all I am saying that maybe making this an enum [instead of a boolean] from the beginning is safer, and more future proof, given that this is something we likely want to add sooner rather than later)

Why would encryption and verity be bogus? I thought verity ensures the files haven't been tampered with, and encryption ensures the disk can't be read without the passphrase. Those concepts seem disjoint to me.

Do you mean that an encrypted verity hash partition doesn't make sense?

Aside from that, this approach looks OK to me.

> Why would encryption and verity be bogus? I thought verity ensures the files haven't been tampered with, and encryption ensures the disk can't be read without the passphrase. Those concepts seem disjoint to me.

But one would use the integrity stuff of LUKS for that, not verity. It's a lot more efficient, since dm-crypt and dm-integrity integrate with each other, and save work.

(and of course, there probably shouldn't be any concept of a "cache" per se in the codebase. i guess all we need is some additoinal fields that store information about the fs/location/verity/results as we acquire the info. And then we should just linearly search among the partitions for matching entries. i.e. just use linear search. I mean, we expect < 100 partitions here, hence a linear search really is not an issue.)

Sorry for late to join the discussion. But, I think the matching logic of data and hash partitions suggested above sounds too complicated for me. Why not to simply introduce e.g. `VerityName=` or so?

50-root.conf
```
[Partition]
Type=root
CopyFiles=/my/source/tree
MakeDirectories=a b c
Format=xfs
VerityType=data
VerityName=foo
```

60-root-verity.conf
```
[Partition]
Type=root-verity
VerityName=foo
VerityType=hash
```

Otherwise, 
- if we have multiple partitions with the same contents configurations (CopyFile=, CopyBlocks=, and etc), then we can not easily guess the result of the matching.
- if we want to change the contents settings, we need to also update the config for verity hash partition. If we have multiple CopyFiles= lines, then it is not friendly for user to make the lists in the two config consistent.

If we introduce VerityName=, then users can easily understand the matching logic, and easily update CopyFile= setting or friends.

Also, how about to check Type= between the matching two partitions?
If Type= is one of the known partition types, then they have to match, e.g. root and root-verity, usr and usr-verity, so on.

> Why not to simply introduce e.g. `VerityName=` or so?

What would the impact of that name be? Would that identifier you'd set here propagate anywhere into the image? Or is it purely intended for matching up the two partitions inside of repart's logic?

If the latter we already have such an identifier: the name of the dropin file. We could in theory use that.

> Also, how about to check Type= between the matching two partitions?
> If Type= is one of the known partition types, then they have to match, e.g. root and root-verity, usr and usr-verity, so on.

Hmm, a major usecase for repart is A/B update scenarios: you have multiple sets of partitions of the same type. That makes finding the counterparts via type uuid alone ugly.

I like the current approach of searching by contents, i.e. by the CopyBlocks=/CopyFiles=/MakeDirectories= values. But I'd also be OK going by drop-in filename. Might even be OK to support both: if in the hash partition definition no dropin file name for the data partition is specified match by CopyBlocks=/CopyFiles=/MakeDirectories=

I quite like the VerityName= approach, it avoids the ugly duplication of all the content options.

> If the latter we already have such an identifier: the name of the dropin file. We could in theory use that.

Hmm, it seems more flexible if we decouple these. That allows changing the filename (for w.e. reason) without having to go and touch unrelated files to change VerityName in each of them. The only thing we really avoid by using the dropin file is that we don't have to specify `VerityName` in one of the definition files. So I'd prefer if we just use `VerityName` with an arbitrary string to couple partitions together. It's intuitive and explicit.

Since `VerityName` is super easy, I'd just support that and wouldn't do the other matching.

> Hmm, a major usecase for repart is A/B update scenarios: you have multiple sets of partitions of the same type. That makes finding the counterparts via type uuid alone ugly.

I don't think Yu is suggesting to use the the partition type UUIDs for matching, just that if we have two matching verity partitions and the data partition type uuid is "root", that we verity that the hash partition type uuid is "root-verity".

I'd go even further and disallow `Type=` if `Verity=hash`, and just infer it from the data partition type UUID..

review_comments: This should be also checked for `dp`.

i'd really hide the uniqueness check in find_verity_sibling() and make it return ENXIO if it can't find the sibling and ENOTUNIQ if not unique

And yeah, I think too it makes sense to cache the result in the partition structure (just add two pointer fields `verity_data_partition` and `verity_hash_partition` to it, no need to avoid wasting a few bytes here), and then use that for the actual verity operatoin instead of searching again

hmm, this should take the priority into consideration.

or maybe better: refuse a configuration where the verity data partition has a different priority than the hash partition already when parsing.

And then add comment here saying that it's safe to drop the sibling regardless of priority since we checked priority matching already before.

hmm, in all checks above you condition if the field is set at all in `p`. I think we shouldn't check that. If it isn't set in `p`, then it should not be set in `q` either. Hence, use just `streq_ptr(p->format, q->format)` as check instead of `p->format && streq(p->format, q->format)`. Or am I missing something?

this doesn't look right. the idea was to show this before we do anything, and in particular show this if we are in dry run mode, so that you can verify everything is in order before you try again. Given that the dry-run check is now done *before* we dump the table the dry-run mode is half useless...

Why would the dry run check be useless now? If we're in dry run, we return 0 early from `context_write_partition_table()` and execute the table logic immediately after that in `run()`.

The only regression would be that we print the table after executing all operations in non dry-run mode. That doesn't seem like a problem to me though, since there's no prompt to ask the user if they want to continue after writing the table now, so even if we write the table early, it's not like the user can do anything with it because repart will immediately go on and write the partition table.
You are right. But also, it's a bit strange if we first say "Applying changes" and only much later say which changes... Sounds better to say first what we are going to change, before we change it.
(I mean, we had various bugs where the application of the changes actually failed, so I think it's kinda nice to report first what are going to do, so that this is visible once we fail)

Not a matter, but dissect_image() requires the length is longer or equals to 128bit.
https://github.com/systemd/systemd/blob/90782fde463ce2af95cc6fff3dcb631e67b2da81/src/shared/dissect-image.c#L243-L244

Yes, but we need it to be at least twice the size to accomodate the boot loader spec, since the first 128 bits need to become the partition uuid for the data partition, and the final 128 bits are needed to become the uuid for the hash partition, that's why I added the assert for twice the size.
So, should we also update the condition in dissect_image()??
I think so?  Unless the verity and data UUID can be the same, not sure if that's intended to work

doesn't need to be done now, but there are a lot of parameters that can be decided by the caller when creating the verity device, including the hash type - should at least be an item in the TODO to add parameters for hash type, FEC, etc
